profile.summary: Carbon-X is a 14.8 billion parameter chat language model that reads DNA and English in the same conversation. You paste raw DNA into a message and ask a question; it answers in English, for example whether a mutation is likely benign or pathogenic, which organism group a sequence comes from, or what the next bases are. It was built from the general-purpose Qwen3-14B model by adding DNA tokens and further training on DNA and biology text.
profile.summary_source_locator: Model card: Model Summary; Vocabulary extension

summary_quotes.text: **Carbon-X** is a 14.8B-parameter decoder-only language model trained jointly on DNA sequences and natural-language text.

You give it raw DNA inside an ordinary chat conversation and it answers in English: it predicts whether mutations are benign or pathogenic, identifies regions that control gene activity, classifies sequences by organism group, predicts the next bases of a sequence, and explains its reasoning.
Carbon-X starts from [Qwen3-14B](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-14B). We add the DNA tokens to its vocabulary with randomly initialised embeddings.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: DNA and text share one token stream in one decoder, with no separate DNA encoder. A hybrid tokeniser keeps Qwen3's BPE vocabulary for text and encodes DNA as non-overlapping 6-mers, so one DNA token covers 6 base pairs; runs of at least 6 A, C, G or T bases are tagged as DNA automatically. Training had four stages. New DNA embeddings were first trained for about 10B tokens with the transformer frozen. The full model was then mid-trained on 302B tokens at sequence length 8,192, a mixture of 55% raw DNA, 20% English, 15% biology text and 10% instruction data. Supervised fine-tuning followed (3 epochs over 20 dataset subsets), then two rounds of GRPO reinforcement learning with code-checked rewards, all with thinking disabled.

quotes.text: DNA and text share a single token stream in a single decoder. There is no separate DNA encoder.
A hybrid tokenizer keeps a BPE vocabulary for text and encodes DNA as non-overlapping 6-mers, so one DNA token covers 6 base pairs.
Runs of at least 6 A/C/G/T bases are wrapped in `<dna>…</dna>` and tokenized as 6-mers.
We then train for about 10B tokens with the transformer body frozen, so that only the new DNA embeddings learn, before unfreezing the whole model.
The full model is then trained for **302B tokens** with a sequence length of 8,192
The mid-trained model is fine-tuned for 3 epochs on a mixture of 20 dataset subsets.
The fine-tuned model is then trained with asynchronous GRPO and verifiable rewards in two rounds, with thinking disabled:

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The released model is HuggingFaceBio/Carbon-X; this page read revision 17de8916. The training pipeline names two intermediate models, Carbon-X-Base (after mid-training) and Carbon-X-SFT (after fine-tuning), and GGUF quantisations exist for llama.cpp. All reported results used thinking disabled and the sampling defaults in generation_config.json (temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, top-k 20), so a result should name the revision, the model variant and any change to these settings. The training recipes, decontamination scripts and evaluation tasks are in the huggingface/carbon repository.

facts.value: Qwen3 decoder-only transformer: 40 layers, hidden size 5120, FFN size 17408, 40 attention heads with grouped-query attention (8 KV heads), head dimension 128, SwiGLU, RMSNorm with QK-norm, RoPE (base 1,000,000), untied embeddings.

facts.label: Inputs
facts.value: Chat messages mixing English and raw DNA. DNA is tokenised as 6-mers plus tail tokens for lengths not divisible by 6; any 6-mer containing a base other than A, C, G or T becomes a single <oov> token.

facts.value: Starts from Qwen3-14B. strengths.text: Asks and answers in plain language, so one model covers variant effect questions, sequence classification and next-base prediction without task-specific heads.

quotes.text: You give it raw DNA inside an ordinary chat conversation and it answers in English

strengths.text: Runs locally on a single 80 GB GPU in bfloat16, with vLLM serving documented, so sensitive sequences can stay on the user's own hardware.
strengths.source_locator: Model card: Model Summary; Serving with vLLM

quotes.text: The weights fit on a single 80 GB GPU in bfloat16, so researchers can keep sensitive or unpublished sequences on their own infrastructure.

strengths.text: By the developers' own evaluation, it averages 66.7% over five DNA benchmarks with thinking disabled, 27 points above its Qwen3-14B starting point.

quotes.text: Across five DNA benchmarks, which cover variant-effect prediction, sequence understanding and next-base prediction, Carbon-X averages **66.7%** with thinking disabled. That is 27 points above Qwen3-14B, the model it starts from

strengths.text: Weights and code are Apache-2.0, and the training recipes and the scripts that decontaminate training data against the evaluation benchmarks are public.

limitations.text: Can miscount bases, confuse coordinates and invent a sequence's identity when context is missing. Splice-site and histone-mark questions remain weak (29.8% and 34.6% on GenomeQA).

quotes.text: The model can miscount bases, confuse coordinates or make incorrect edits
The model may invent a sequence's identity or function when the prompt does not give enough information.
Splice-site and histone-mark questions remain weak (29.8% and 34.6% on GenomeQA).

limitations.text: Not trained to design sequences; quality degrades for long DNA generation. Ambiguous bases such as N collapse a whole 6-mer into one <oov> token.

quotes.text: Quality degrades when the model is asked to generate long DNA sequences. Carbon-X reads and explains existing sequences. It was not trained to design new ones.

run_guide.summary: Install Transformers, load Carbon-X in bfloat16 on a GPU and ask it whether a variant is likely benign or pathogenic.
prerequisites: A CUDA GPU; the card says the weights fit on a single 80 GB GPU in bfloat16.
Transformers v5 or later, and PyTorch.
Hugging Face Hub access on first load (the tokeniser downloads its BPE vocabulary). The tokeniser is custom code loaded with trust_remote_code=True.
Weights and code are Apache-2.0 and not gated.

steps.title: Install
steps.explanation: The model card's install command. The card requires Transformers v5 or later.

quotes.text: Carbon-X requires Transformers v5 or later.

steps.title: Ask a variant question
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer

model_id = "HuggingFaceBio/Carbon-X"

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id, trust_remote_code=True)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_id, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map="cuda")

messages = [
    {
        "role": "user",
        "content": (
            "Reference: ATGGTGCATCTGACTCCTGAGGAGAAGTCTGCCGTTACTGCCCTGTGGGGCAAGG\n"
            "Variant:   ATGGTGCATCTGACTCCTGTGGAGAAGTCTGCCGTTACTGCCCTGTGGGGCAAGG\n\n"
            "Is this variant likely to be benign or pathogenic? Explain your reasoning."
        ),
    }
]
inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
    messages,
    add_generation_prompt=True,
    enable_thinking=False,
    return_tensors="pt",
    return_dict=True,
).to(model.device)

outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=1024)
print(tokenizer.decode(outputs[0][inputs["input_ids"].shape[1]:], skip_special_tokens=True))
PY
steps.explanation: The model card's Python example, unchanged, wrapped in a shell heredoc. It downloads the weights on first run and keeps thinking disabled, as the developers recommend.

quotes.text: Carbon-X was post-trained and evaluated with `enable_thinking=False`, and we recommend keeping it that way.

outputs: The model's English answer on whether the variant is likely benign or pathogenic, with its reasoning, printed to the terminal. Sampling uses the defaults in generation_config.json, so the text can differ between runs.
